Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Vignette:
Amir is a 54-year-old software engineer who lives alone in a quiet suburban apartment, a place he chose specifically because it has no shared corridors and a deadbolt on every door. Five years ago, he was the last person leaving his office building late one evening when a security guard—a man in a dark uniform whose name tag he never saw—stopped him in the stairwell, claimed a “check” was needed, and then assaulted him behind a steel door. During the attack, Amir heard sirens outside, growing then fading, and he remembers silently begging for them to stop and come up the stairs. They didn’t. Afterwards, he walked home in a daze, showered until the water ran cold, and never told anyone at work. He was certain he had done something wrong—staying late, agreeing to the check, not fighting back—and that reporting it would only prove he had invited it. Nothing has been done to the man; as far as Amir knows, that uniform still patrols the building.

In the months that followed, Amir began to notice that his own body was no longer under his control. A car backfiring on the street would send him diving toward a wall; the wail of a distant ambulance would make his mouth go dry and his hands shake. He stopped walking past the office complex entirely, taking a bus that adds forty minutes to his commute. He also started avoiding any situation where he might be alone with a man—no more elevators, no more after-hours meetings, no more one-on-one code reviews. The sight of a police cruiser or a security uniform made him cross the street, and he began to dread any interaction with authority figures, including his own team lead, whose firm voice reminded him of the guard’s “just a routine check.” At work, he refused a promotion because it would have required monthly presentations in a room with a male department head. He told himself the extra money wasn’t worth the panic, though his bank account began to shrink with the unpaid leave he took after every close call.

Over time, Amir’s world shrank. He started scanning every doorway, every parked van, every group of men on a sidewalk. He carried a small folding knife, though he knew it was useless, and he only felt truly safe inside his own apartment with the blinds down and the door triple-locked. Even there, a sudden siren from a passing emergency vehicle would make him press his back against the wall, heart hammering, certain that someone was about to break in. He had long since stopped feeling the normal emotions he used to take for granted—no real joy when his niece visited, no anger at a rude driver, only a flat hum of vigilance and exhaustion. He believed he had lost something permanent, that the man in the uniform had taken not just his safety but his capacity to feel like a person.

What finally brought Amir into therapy was a morning when a fire engine screamed past his building while he was standing in the kitchen. He dropped his coffee, slid to the floor, and stayed there for forty minutes, sure that the sirens were coming for him, that the assault was happening again even though he was alone. Later that day, his sister—who had noticed his withdrawal and his refusal to visit her family’s home because her husband was there—called and said, calmly, that she missed her brother. That evening, Amir searched online for a therapist who specialized in trauma, still half-convinced that talking about it would make it worse, that the shame would swallow him. But what frightened him most was the idea that if he didn’t try, he would spend the rest of his life flinching at horns and hiding behind locked doors, certain that no justice existed and that he had only himself to blame. He wanted to feel something other than fear, even if he no longer believed he could.
